problems: E05 reports that none of the SCREEN core biosamples match the stated LNCaP context. Its zero-of-170 enhancer/promoter-like result is not a tested-negative result for LNCaP; context-specific activity remains unknown.

The RFX6 target assignment is indirect. Intronic location, L2G scores, and E27 gene–disease evidence do not establish that this cCRE regulates RFX6; E06 instead reports contacts to VGLL2 and an adipose FAM162B eQTL.

The binding models predict opposite allelic preferences across candidates: HOXB13 favors T, whereas AR, GATA2, VDR-family, and NR1I3-family predictions favor C. The prostate cancer association reports C as the effect allele, but no evidence establishes how any binding change affects RFX6 expression or disease risk.
Nearby ChIP peaks support local occupancy, but none of the cited results demonstrates allele-specific occupancy or a causal variant-to-gene effect.

checks.why: An independent check for a variant-overlapping HOXB13 ChIP peak in the relevant prostate context could strengthen or weaken the occupancy component of H1.
An independent check for a variant-overlapping AR ChIP peak in the relevant prostate context could strengthen or weaken the occupancy component of H2.
Disease-association evidence for RFX6 could change how strongly RFX6 is prioritized as the target gene, a weak link shared by all five chains.

critique.next_experiment: In LNCaP clone FGC, create isogenic T and C alleles and measure allele-dependent HOXB13, AR, and GATA2 occupancy together with RFX6 expression. This would test whether the predicted binding differences occur in cells and whether the variant changes the proposed target gene.

games.reason: HOXB13 is better supported at the binding step: its own model strongly favors ref T (E13), and it has a summit 11 bp from the variant plus ReMap peaks in LNCaP (E13, E25). VDR’s own mapped model favors alt C, but the predicted effect is weaker and its summit is farther away, at 38 bp (E14). C is the reported prostate-cancer risk allele (E07), which is directionally consistent with B’s binding prediction, but the evidence does not establish that binding mediates disease risk; it does not outweigh A’s stronger, more direct occupancy evidence.

HOXB13 is supported more directly: its own QBiC-SELEX model strongly favors ref T, and it is highly expressed in LNCaP with a ChIP-seq summit 11 bp from the variant, including matching-context ReMap peaks. VDR has a nearby summit, but its expression is much lower and the reported nuclear-receptor model is NR2F6, not VDR; its alt-favoring prediction is therefore less directly tied to VDR. The shared element, target-gene, and phenotype evidence does not distinguish the chains.
